item.title: Try, Try Again: Why Failure Is Necessary for Success
item.description:
Resilience

Try, Try Again: Why Failure Is Necessary for Success

New research shows that failure in life goes hand-in-hand with success in life.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Successful people can often recount many failures that they encountered along the way.
  • The ability to bounce back from failures in life is part of our evolved psychological resilience.
  • A new study supports this conception; failure in life and success in life seem to go hand-in-hand.
Source: Pineapple Mango / Pexels

While I hardly identify as being hugely successful in my profession, I guess I've done alright over the years. Most people who know about my work know about my successes (including 10 academic books, over 100 peer-reviewed journal articles and book chapters, this award and that award, etc.).

Sure, I've done OK. But what I don't tend to amplify out into the universe are the many failures that I have encountered so frequently across my career. Consider the following:

  • I got into less than half the Ph.D. programs I'd applied for. Way less!
  • For nearly every published paper I have, I can recount at least one rejection from another publisher.
  • For every book I've published, there are multiple "we're sorry, but your book idea does not meet our mission; we wish you luck" situations.
  • When I started my academic career, I applied to well over 100 academic jobs. Most of them totally ghosted me.

And this is to say nothing of the failures in my personal life over the last half century...

That said, like many of us, I learned about the importance of failing in life as a critical part of learning. If at first you don't succeed, try, try again. This all speaks to the issue of resilience.

Resilience in Evolutionary Perspective

The psychology of resilience has an interesting evolution-based take. In writing about the nature of evolved psychological adaptations, renowned evolutionary psychologist, David Buss (2024), Buss likens psychological adaptations to callouses on one's foot or hand. The capacity for callouses exists, regardless of whether any callouses actually emerge in one's life. Callous-producing mechanisms only build callouses if certain experiences have taken place.

If you have just started running long distances for the first time, you'll likely notice callouses on certain parts of your feet. If you take up tennis, you will find callouses on your hands and fingers. Etc. This is all normal—and these callouses help to provide long-term protection for your skin.

We can think of psychological resilience in a parallel way. Greg Lukianoff and Jonathan Haidt (2018) argue that being sheltered from adverse experiences in life offers short-term benefits—but these benefits often come with long-term problems.

The ability to deal with adversity relies partly on one's experiences with adversity. From this perspective, sheltering a child from adversity too much during their upbringing may actually lead to lowered resilience in adulthood.

Drawing on these ideas, in our book Positive Evolutionary Psychology (Geher & Wedberg, 2022), Nicole Wedberg and I present a thesis regarding the relationship between failures and successes in one's life. We essentially put forward an ironic prediction: More failures in life may predict more successes. This hypothesis, rooted in the evolutionary psychology of resilience, might help shed light on how people may be able to deal with those inevitable failures in life in healthy ways.

The Success Study

In a recent study on this topic that was spearheaded by my student collaborator (Kardas et al., 2025), my research team asked the questions as to whether (a) the number of major failures that one perceives in their life experiences tend to go hand-in-hand with the number of major successes that one perceives in their life experiences. Further, we sought to ascertain whether (b) the perceived impact of one's history of successes in life goes hand-in-hand with the perceived impact of one's history of failures in life.

In a study of nearly 200 English-speaking adults, we found strong evidence for each. In this study, we asked people to think about and list as many substantial successes in life as they could. We also asked them to rate each success in terms of the impact that it has had on their life, and we asked the same kinds of questions to obtain an index of total number of substantial failures as well as the impact that they believed these failures to have had on their lives.

The "failure is predictive of success" hypothesis was supported. People who reported a lot of successes also reported a lot of failures (while those who reported few successes tended to report few failures). Findings based on the impact of success and failure were consistent with this pattern: People who reported that successes had impacted them largely also tended to report that failures had impacted them largely. And vice versa.

Bottom Line: We Don't Have to Fear Failure

Since we were little, so many of us have been told that failure is OK and, in fact, that it is necessary for learning and for ultimately succeeding in life. Taking an evolutionary perspective to this topic, a recent study by my research team (Kardas et al., 2025) provides strong evidence for this age-old adage.

Participants in this study described successes and failures in their lives along two dimensions (total number; perceived impact). In our analysis, we found that people who reported more successes in life also reported more failures in life, and vice versa. What's more, people who reported that successes impacted their lives a lot also tended to report that failures impacted their lives a lot, and vice versa.

So next time you fail at something in your life (mess up at work, fail to get a promotion, upset your partner without meaning to, get a speeding ticket with a mile of getting home, lose your phone, crack an egg on the kitchen floor, unwittingly insult a friend, fail a college exam, lose at trivia, go around all day with your shirt inside-out, etc.), it may benefit you to remember that failure is not only part of life—it is an essential kind of experience that ultimately predicts success in one's future. Our psychological resilience evolved this way.

Don't beat yourself up over that recent failure. We all make mistakes. Get back up on that horse—each of these cliches actually is rooted in deep truths about the human condition. In life, success and failure actually do go hand-in-hand.

item.title: Moms, Daughters, and the Sisterhood of the “Right-Sized” Pants
item.description:
Social Life

Moms, Daughters, and the Sisterhood of the “Right-Sized” Pants

Moms can play an important role in college women's sorority decisions.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Our group memberships can powerfully influence our behaviors, so they should be chosen with care.
  • Sororities offer the possibility of belongingness and lifelong friendship.
  • Sororities can also foster an unhealthy focus on appearance and negative body image.
  • Moms can play an important role in their daughters' decisions by supporting and modeling critical thinking.

A young woman’s first year of college is an exciting time full of new experiences, new friends, and new independence. Naturally, parents want this to be a meaningful and memorable moment in their student’s transition to early adulthood. And during the fall semester, many prospective students are touring their campuses and considering whether they will join a sorority—the process known as “Rush.” Media reports highlight parents becoming heavily invested in helping their daughters gain membership into their desired sorority. There is even a thriving industry of sorority “rush consultants” who promise to help young ladies receive bids from the campus groups they desire—for a fee.

What types of memories and connections do we want them to make?

Recent news headlines have reignited conversations on the toxic culture and extreme behaviors that membership in Greek life can entail. Although much of the recent attention has focused on fraternities and sexual assault, sororities often have their own toxic cultures, especially around the topics of physical appearance and food restriction.

For example, we know that sorority membership affects women’s BMI; sorority members have lower BMIs than non-sorority members (Doney et al., 2023). Women who participate in rush tend to engage in more self-objectification and have more disordered eating behaviors than women who do not (Rolnik et al., 2010) and both tendencies are well-known correlates of negative body image. Additionally, sorority sisters report a heavy focus on, and pressures around, physical appearance and compliance with unrealistic beauty ideals. These pressures are felt especially strongly when wearing clothing that associates them with their group (Skubisz et al., 2023).

Conformity pressures and group membership

Group influence is powerful and can encourage behaviors that would otherwise be unthinkable to an individual. At the heart of a group’s influence is a process known as deindividuation, a psychological state in which people temporarily lose sight of their personal beliefs and principles because they feel immersed in the group. This idea has been around a long time (e.g., Le Bon, 1895), although the term was first coined in 1952 (Festinger et al., 1952). Well-known experiments (e.g., Milgram, 1974; Burger, 2009) have taught us that it is crucial to choose one’s group membership wisely; otherwise, people may find themselves behaving in ways that are at odds with their true values.

Is sorority membership a bad idea?

Not necessarily! Parents understandably want their children to find belongingness in their new environments, and sororities can offer this social connection. Overall, students affiliated with Greek life report less loneliness and greater feelings of belonging than students who are not (Reeves-Doyle et al., 2026). This important benefit of sorority membership may be seen as worth the risk of exposure to some harmful social norms.

Not all young women are equally connected within the sisterhood, however. Prochnow and colleagues (2021) found that the level of social connectedness within a sorority is an important consideration—and that sorority sisters who are less close and connected within the sisterhood are more vulnerable to body dissatisfaction than those who are more deeply connected within the group. So, if a young woman doesn't make deep and meaningful connections in her sisterhood, the belonging benefit may not be worth the risk of the toxic appearance culture after all.

What's a mom to do?

Even though your daughter is now at her university building a new social network, she still needs you, but perhaps in a way you haven’t considered. Your daughter is a young adult now and doesn't need your direct intervention in her social life (e.g., helping her seek a particular group membership because you found belongingness in that group). Instead, she needs you to model critical-thinking skills and a strong commitment to prioritizing what is best for one's personal mental and physical health, even when that is not the most popular choice.

In our book, Beyond Body Positive: A Mother’s Science-Based Guide for Helping Girls Build a Healthy Body Image (2024), we discuss a great deal of research suggesting that a daughter’s body image is built through social interactions, and that moms have an enduring influence in their daughters’ thoughts, feelings, and behaviors.

We can help our daughters make healthy choices about the groups they join by asking them questions rather than outright saying "No" or "Yes" to membership. For example, we can ask her what she is looking for in a group and why. We can ask how a group embodies her own values and priorities. We can help her reason through her decisions by playing a supportive role, rather than a directive one.

The mother-daughter relationship is the partnership of a lifetime. Maintaining healthy body image in a heavily appearance-focused culture will require self-awareness, agency, intentionality, and commitment to personal health. Moms can model these behaviors for their daughters' pursuit of truly healthy and fulfilling sisterhood.

item.title: The Circular Logic of "Autistic Burnout" and "Low-Demand Parenting"
item.description:
Autism

The Circular Logic of "Autistic Burnout" and "Low-Demand Parenting"

Two untested ideas can prop each other up so that nothing can prove them wrong.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Autistic burnout in children and low-demand parenting each have little empirical support.
  • Together, each idea is taken as proof of the other, and a calmer home is mistaken for recovery.
  • When resisting makes a demand disappear, especially if a screen follows, a child learns that resisting works.
  • SPACE, which coaches parents to reduce accommodation, offers a tested alternative.

Social media posts like the following appear nearly every day in parent support groups for neurodivergent kids:

“Mornings have become a battle because my son refuses to go to school. I tried everything. Therapy, medication. Nothing helped. He’s getting worse, and now he barely talks to us. He spends all day in his room, and screens are the only thing that keeps him calm. We’ve stopped asking him to do anything because it always ends up in a fight. What should I do?”

Often, the advice that follows nearly always says the same thing: “Your son is in burnout, and you should lower demands so he can recover.”

Is letting neurodivergent kids "rest" really the answer?
Source: Author: AI Generated

This sounds plausible, even compassionate. But the advice rests on two ideas that have very little empirical support, and research exists that challenges both.

The First Idea: Autistic Burnout in Children

Burnout is an important idea when it comes to autistic adults, who describe chronic exhaustion and reduced sensory tolerance resulting from accumulated stress (Raymaker et al., 2020). Adult definitions and questionnaires now exist.

However, autistic burnout in children has not been well studied. A 2025 review found most autistic burnout research participants were white, female, late-diagnosed adults (Ali et al., 2025). Research on children consists of a few small interview studies and chart reviews.

There is no validated child measure of burnout, and even burnout in adults hasn't been reliably distinguished from depression. In one sample, 98 percent of participants scored above the depression cutoff (Arnold et al., 2023).

Of course, children, like anyone else, can become exhausted. But applying an adult concept to a demand-avoidant eight-year-old is a different matter altogether.

The Second Idea: Low Demand Parenting

The second idea is that when a child is in burnout, social media tells parents to reduce “demands” (i.e., increase accommodations), which allows a child to recover from chronic overwhelm. The idea is appealing because when demand-avoidant children are expected to do less, conflict in the family is reduced.

However, despite its widespread popularity, there is no evidence that lowering demands is effective for reducing demand avoidance. The one study we have so far that tested the approach (Carlozzi et al., 2025) found it reduced parental stress, but it was largely ineffective in improving demand-avoidant symptoms and behavior.

The Circular Connection Between "Burnout" and Lower Demands

Believing a child to be in burnout justifies lowering expectations, and the reduced conflict that comes from lowering expectations is used as proof that the label was right and the approach is effective. That’s a loop.

Some kids might get better eventually simply because time passes and they mature, which is used as further evidence to support both ideas. But what if they don’t? Suppose a child continues to languish in their bedroom on a screen, rarely leaves the house, and their world gradually shrinks. Social media would argue that the child is still in burnout and just needs more time and more “rest.”

Every outcome confirms the circular argument, creating a belief system that resists other ways of conceptualizing the problem and getting the child a different kind of help.

The Problem with Lowering Expectations

When resisting demands results in lowered expectations, this is a classic example of negative reinforcement, a well-studied concept in behavioral psychology. Demand-avoidant behavior can be extremely persuasive. If a child resists hard enough and parents gradually stop asking things of them, this strengthens the very behavior parents are hoping to change.

This is just a basic reinforcement principle, but it is largely unknown or discussed in parent-led spaces.

The Research on Accommodations

In contrast to autistic burnout, there is a substantial body of research on what happens to a child’s anxiety when parents accommodate heavily.

For example, Macul Ferreira de Barros and his colleagues (2020) found that accommodation helped explain why children struggled more in daily life (school, friendships, and daily routines). Accommodation can also become a bidirectional loop that grows over time. One study found that when a teen's anxiety increased, parents accommodated even more, and that added accommodation resulted in even more anxiety (Bertelsen et al., 2023).

This is true for autistic children as well. In a trial of 167 anxious autistic children, 81 percent of parents reduced expectations at least weekly, and children with more accommodation before treatment had more anxiety afterward (Frank et al., 2022).

If Not Low-Demand, Then What?

In the anxiety space, one promising treatment is SPACE (Supportive Parenting for Anxious Childhood Emotions), developed at the Yale Child Study Center. SPACE recognizes that parental accommodation is contributing to or even worsening a child's anxiety. Essentially, it is the opposite of low-demand parenting, and the treatment is implemented only through the parents (Lebowitz et al., 2020).

SPACE begins by identifying accommodations in the family and then develops a strategy to systematically reduce them. Kids are told in advance what changes the parents are going to make, along with supportive statements conveying optimism (“I know some of these changes might be hard at first, but I'm confident you can handle it”).

Invariably, kids resist these changes at the beginning. They can get angry, escalate, become aggressive, and say things like “If you really loved me, you wouldn’t make me do this” (Lebowitz et al., 2014). SPACE draws on nonviolent resistance, and parents don't argue, threaten, or punish.

In a randomized trial of 124 anxious children aged 7 to 14, SPACE was as effective as CBT delivered directly to the child, and it reduced parental accommodation more (Lebowitz et al., 2020). A small pilot in autistic children aged 6 to 10 found it also reduced anxiety and accommodation, changes that were sustained at two months (Rozenblat et al., 2025).

Intensive Family-Focused Therapy (IFFT)

My clinic takes a related approach with demand-avoidant children. Along with reducing accommodation, we gradually reintroduce expectations, starting with ones that are easiest to change, such as a child helping around the house or speaking kindly to family.

Children often resist, as they do in SPACE, so we pair expectations with incentives: Rather than unlimited screen time, for example, screens become available once chores are done. Also like SPACE, change is explained matter-of-factly as a new household routine rather than as something punitive. The principle is the same: support the child through a manageable challenge rather than removing it.

Data from our clinic's standardized outcome measures is quite promising. Demand-avoidant behavior improves substantially, age-typical expectations are restored, and the child's anxiety is simultaneously reduced.

Getting Out of the Loop

Some children need a lighter load for a time; that’s not in dispute. But it’s essential to distinguish temporary exhaustion from ongoing avoidance.

One way to tell the difference is the length of time it takes a child to recover. A child spending months (and sometimes years) in their bedroom is an indication that something’s not working and it's time for a different approach.

Temporarily reducing conflict is appealing, but it’s not evidence of recovery. If nothing is changing, consider finding a clinician experienced in treating demand avoidance who doesn’t advocate for a low-demand approach.

You're not giving up compassion. You’re replacing one narrative that says “I believe you can’t” with one that says “I believe you can.”

item.title: Our Children Deserve More Than Our Anger
item.description:
Anger

Our Children Deserve More Than Our Anger

What growing up in the Central Valley taught me about fear and leadership

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Partisan identity can shape which facts we accept, even when we believe we are judging fairly.
  • A neighborhood's reputation cannot tell us whether the children living there feel safe or supported.
  • Delano farmworkers and the Panthers paired resistance with practical care for their communities.
  • Forgiveness takes different forms; healing can also change what the next generation experiences.

I grew up in a valley that fed this country while children nearby went hungry. My grandparents worked in the fields, then walked into stores where people judged them for not speaking English. They helped put food on people’s tables, yet still had to prove they belonged in the very place they called home.

By fourteen, I was homeless. I learned survival before I finished being a child. Police harassed me and others in my neighborhood. At school, adults saw how I looked and reacted, then asked what I was carrying. I grew up feeling that strangers knew my story better than I did.

I wasn’t in a gang. Many children around me weren’t either. Some avoided violence; others sought protection or belonging in gangs, despite the dangers. Families deserved safe streets. So did children growing up on them.

Sanger, a farming town near Fresno, obtained gang injunctions in 2003 and 2012. Prosecutors credited the first with fewer calls for service. Families feared gang violence; children like me also feared being mistaken for it. The numbers couldn’t tell us who had a safe place to go or an adult willing to listen.

A neighborhood could be called dangerous while the children living there were themselves in danger. We saw the label before we saw the child.

What Pain Can Teach Us to See

I know anger. It can stay with you long after the moment that caused it. When you’ve felt unseen, someone who stands up for your people can feel like the first person who sees you. That loyalty carries love. It can also make us reluctant to question what happens in our name.

A confrontation appears on a phone. Before hearing the whole story, we know whom to praise. Psychologists Jay Van Bavel and Andrea Pereira describe how political party identity can shape which information we accept. Their model concerns partisanship, but it raises a question about my own loyalty: Am I defending what happened, or what I need to believe happened?

Jiddu Krishnamurti asked whether we can clearly observe another person when our memories and prejudices interfere. When I feel most certain, I ask what I still haven’t understood.

I don’t want our people to be silent in the face of injustice. Silence can leave families unprotected and institutions unaccountable. Protest, organizing, and demands for change matter. The US government can arrest and detain; residents challenging it cannot. Those powers are not equal. Still, we must ask whether our actions protect people or leave someone else carrying more fear.

What Our People Built

In 1965, Filipino farmworkers led by Larry Itliong struck Delano. Mexican and Mexican American workers joined eight days later, defying divisions growers had exploited. Later retellings often overlooked Filipino organizers.

Workers shared a union hall and strike kitchen, sustained a boycott, and won contracts in 1970. When I think of my grandparents, I picture workers who helped feed the country needing someone to feed them so they could return to the picket lines. Care sustained resistance; it did not replace it.

The Black Panther Party confronted state violence and organized free breakfasts for children. In 1969, FBI director J. Edgar Hoover called the program potentially the greatest threat to efforts to neutralize the Party. Its contradictions and government repression deserve study. Still, children were hungry, and people organized a meal.

Luis Valdez founded El Teatro Campesino on the Delano picket lines. He later incorporated In Lak’ech into Pensamiento Serpentino, crediting Maya scholar Domingo Martínez Paredes for the teaching. Tú eres mi otro yo. You are my other me.

Those words became harder for me to live than to admire.

What Healing Asked of Me

My brother Sammy Mercado was missing for six months. We later learned he had been shot and murdered. There is a particular cruelty in not knowing where your brother is, then having to live with knowing how he died. Nothing makes that loss acceptable.

I wrestled with forgiving the person who killed him. Accountability still mattered. I wanted my love for Sammy, not hatred for his killer, to shape what came next. In a 2016 study, sociologist Kristen Hourigan (now Kristen Discola) found different understandings of forgiveness among homicide survivors, often shaped by family or faith. Forgiveness was my path, never a demand on another grieving family.

I cannot tell you what would have prevented Sammy’s murder. I can tell you what I do now. I work with schools to help young people find caring adults and possibilities beyond survival. I want to reach children who remind me of Sammy, and children adults have already decided are dangerous. I cannot know which opportunities might interrupt violence. That uncertainty cannot become an excuse to offer none.

Shawn Ginwright’s healing-centered engagement calls us to change the conditions that produce suffering and to care for adults’ healing, too. I call these compounded burdens Poverty 4x: poverty, trauma, racism, and cultural erasure. We count arrests and absences, but do we know who needs shelter or an adult who believes in them?

Now I sit at tables where adults once made decisions about children like me. When a child arrives with a label, I need to learn what is happening in their life before deciding what to do next. Healing that stays inside me is not enough. It must change what I do with a seat at that table, especially when my anger feels justified.

At fourteen, I didn’t need someone to make the world afraid of my neighborhood. I needed someone to see that I was afraid of it. I needed somewhere to sleep and adults who saw beyond how I had learned to survive.

Would the fourteen-year-old boy I once was have felt safe, seen, and worthy in the presence of the adult I have become?

My titles cannot answer that. Neither can my intentions. The children standing in front of me will live with the answer.

In Lak’ech.

item.title: Why You Can Feel Lonely Even When You Are Loved
item.description:
Loneliness

Why You Can Feel Lonely Even When You Are Loved

Connection can relieve loneliness without reaching every hidden part of the self.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Loneliness is shaped by the quality of connection, not simply by the presence of other people.
  • Research finds that married adults can remain lonely within their closest relationship.
  • Self-silencing can leave important needs and vulnerabilities unwitnessed for years.
  • Identifying the precise connection we need can turn shame into curiosity and conversation.

I liked Steve.

He and Jane had been married for 50 years. He wasn’t cruel or emotionally absent, and Jane did not describe their marriage as dysfunctional. There was love, companionship, and loyalty between them.

Jane and I sat in the living room for our interview. She waited for Steve to drive away in his Mercedes.

“I met him—Steve—at one of the posh political functions my father used to organize,” she told me. “We only went out once, and the next time I met him, he said, ‘I think we should get married,’ and I said, ‘You better go and see my father then.’ I was 18!”

“My father said, ‘I have decided to invite all the Commonwealth ambassadors.’ I had no choice. We had this enormous, extravagant, beautiful wedding. I wouldn’t have dared object! My father would have gone mad!” she continued.

She went on to describe a materially privileged married life and a loving husband, but also an underlying sense that she’d always had to edit herself around the decisions and wishes of others. Her feelings, desires, and needs tended to take a back seat.

She had recently been attacked and robbed while out walking near the retirement community where they lived. She’d noticed a man lingering near the entrance and approached him to ask whether he needed help.

“I thought he looked lost,” she explained. “So, I walked over and said, ‘Are you alright? Do you need some help?’ And then... he simply attacked me.” After a struggle in which she was roughly pushed to the ground and had her handbag and keys stolen, she made her way back to the community reception.

She leaned closer to me. “You know,” she said, “I was so badly bruised afterwards. My shoulder, my arm, my leg… I was covered in bruises.”

“Steve still doesn’t know about any of that. And he’s not going to.”

I was surprised.

“Oh, don’t worry. That’s exactly how I wanted it,” she continued. “I didn’t want to burden him. I’ve always dealt with things like this myself.”

Jane’s marriage was not, as far as I could tell, emotionally cold or unloving. It seemed clear to me that Steve cared for her deeply. And yet, something inside her appeared unable to trust that there might be space for her suffering and vulnerability. Perhaps Steve would have received these parts of Jane with tenderness. Or perhaps he wouldn’t.

Part of her loneliness lay in the fact that she had learned not to risk finding out.

Love can soften loneliness without removing the private distance between two inner worlds.
Source: AI-generated image created by Sam Carr using OpenAI, 2026.

Why Love Doesn’t Always Mean the End of Loneliness

Listening carefully to people’s experiences of loneliness, I have learned that it so often lives inside close human relationships too.

There is a dominant narrative around loneliness that tends to position it as the inverse of connection. That is, if you’re socially connected, in a relationship, married, or surrounded by love, then you’re somehow insured against loneliness.

Many of us imagine that when we find love, a partner, or more friends, our loneliness will evaporate. In my experience, while there’s no doubt that human connection can relieve certain forms of loneliness enormously, it does not necessarily eradicate loneliness itself.

This is because loneliness cannot be reduced to the simple absence of people, or even of love. Researchers commonly understand it as a discrepancy between the relationships we have and those we desire. In experiential terms, it is the felt distance between the connection we have and the connection we need. That distance can be felt both inside and outside human relationships.

How Loneliness Changes Shape

Before entering a relationship, for example, our loneliness may focus acutely on the perceived absence of a partner. We may long for someone with whom to share our days, our bodies, our thoughts, or the unwitnessed details of our lives. The imagined relationship becomes the answer to our loneliness.

Yet research confirms that even married adults can experience loneliness, and inside relationships other, more particular forms of loneliness can take root.

We may no longer be lonely for somebody, but for our partner to understand a particular part of us. We might long for a conversation that never quite happens as we need it to, for a form of intimacy our partner cannot offer, or for permission to reveal a part of ourselves we keep concealed.

It’s as though loneliness is often not eradicated by connection but transmuted by it. Sometimes, the closer we are to a loved one, the more acutely we feel the limits of how far they are ultimately able to enter our inner world. Closeness can soften our existential loneliness, but it can also make the remaining distance between two people more visible.

Of course, relational loneliness can sometimes indicate neglect, coercion, or incompatibility - but it does not automatically prove that love is absent or that a relationship has failed.

What This Shift in Understanding Makes Possible

Recognising this possibility can release us from the expectation that the presence of another person will automatically eradicate loneliness. It allows us to approach the feeling with curiosity rather than shame, without immediately concluding that something is wrong with us or the relationship.

Instead of wondering: How can I possibly be lonely when I have a partner, a family, or people who love me? we might ask: What form of connection am I longing for here? What part of me feels unable to reach—or be reached by—the other?

On the afternoon we spoke, Jane seemed to need a space in which the quietly suppressed parts of her could finally be expressed, given words, and witnessed. Loneliness inside love is not necessarily a verdict on the love. Sometimes it is an invitation to let a previously hidden part of us become known.

I explore Jane’s story more fully in Loneliness Also Lives Inside Love at The Inner Room, where I write free essays about loneliness and the quieter dimensions of inner life. You’re warmly invited to subscribe.

item.title: I Lost My Family to Cancer and Drugs; Here’s How I Survived
item.description:
Grief

I Lost My Family to Cancer and Drugs; Here’s How I Survived

Personal Perspective: Finding a way to trust life again and accept a painful duality.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Those of us who have experienced traumatic loss must now accept a profound and painful duality.
  • There is no timeframe nor rigid structure to the lasting experience of traumatic loss grief.
  • Regaining trust of life is one of the ways we can find some sense of healing.

In 2019, I was cleaning out my mother’s house after the overdose death of my brother, Matthew, who had been occupying the house after my mother’s death from cancer the year before. As I carried a load of old pots and pans out to the dumpster in the driveway, a nosy neighbor walked up and told me, “You’re the last man standing.” I suppose it was meant as supportive, but it left me feeling isolated, alone, and defined by loss. Following the loss of my other brother and Matthew’s twin, Joseph, from a heroin overdose in 2009 and the estrangement from my father around 2015, I felt utterly alone in the wake of what I viewed as an unmitigated disaster of a family. Sure, I was the last one left, but that also meant I was now the one to clean up the mess, figure everything out, and find some way to continue on with my own life.

False Coping Through Busyness

I admit, though, in the immediate aftermath of the collective loss, I coped relatively well. There was a lot to do, and I was busy. From straightening out my brother’s finances to settling my mother’s estate to rummaging through a house full of family history, I barely had time to breathe, let alone grieve. I felt purposeful and determined. Speaking with others who have endured catastrophic, traumatic loss, I find increasingly that this phenomenon is common, as so many of us can adaptively turn to solution-focus in the face of tragedy as if we are flipping a switch. The problem is that this state of busyness does not last, and, eventually, the dust settles.

After the Dust Settles

There comes a point where you have crossed every “t” and dotted every “i”—you’ve secured the death certificates, you’ve closed the accounts, you’ve cleaned out the house—and this is when the weight of loss hits you. The freedom that your mind now has often turns to thoughts of anger, depression, denial—you know the rest. What we do after the dust settles says a lot about how we are really coping. I did not cope well once I was less busy; though I never fell into the addictive patterns to which my brothers succumbed, I unquestionably behaved recklessly, engaged in substance use to an unhealthy degree, and acted out of character in many ways. It was as though I was no longer myself. I can recall having a vivid feeling of standing alone on a planet somewhere in space, completely isolated on an alien surface. That image encapsulates the emotional experience of that time in my life.

Dreams and Intrusions

People often think that if you are going to work, living your life, getting through the day, you must be “over it.” Let me assure you, your subconscious has a lot to say about that notion. Many nights, I dreamt of a recurring theme: Family members would be at a physical distance from me, but I could see them and speak to them. They, however, were unaware of my presence or my attempts to communicate. It was as though I had no voice, or they had no ability to hear, or some combination of the two. Certainly, lines can be drawn psychologically, and Carl Jung would likely have a field day with interpretation of these dreams. In my mind, it’s simple: I still had things to say to them; I still wanted to communicate and connect, but their dreamlike ignorance of me cemented the reality that it could never happen. I would also (and still do) experience waking moments of intrusion—for instance, I see someone in my peripheral vision that resembles my mother, and I think for just a millisecond, “It’s her.” These intrusions are not visible to the bystander who observes you as coping well and being “over it.”

Accepting Duality

So, it has been 17 years since the death of Joseph and nearly 10 since the deaths of Mom and Matthew. Does that mean I am over it? That I am healed? Yes and no. I no longer persistently feel like the “last man standing,” but things can easily trigger that feeling, and it can come back and hit me hard. My son will never have a maternal grandmother nor uncles on his dad’s side; it is recognitions like this that can pop up unexpectedly and bring the loss rushing back, even years or decades later. So, I continue to work at accepting a strange and painful duality: My family of origin no longer exists, but my current family (myself, my wife, and my son) is beautifully intact. One side of that hurts like hell; the other feels almost too good to be true. It is a strange thing to balance, but I suspect I am far from alone in experiencing this profound juxtaposition.

Trusting Life Again

In the face of traumatic loss, you stop trusting that life can be OK. You prepare for the worst, you brace yourself, you live stiffened and tightened up, like a boxer bracing for the next gut punch. It takes a lot to start trusting life again. I wish I could tell you how I regained my trust, but I doubt I could simplistically explain it here. Gradually, though, life began to feel less treacherous. Two things I know have helped: not hiding this history of loss deep within myself and accepting that not everyone can understand, despite my wish that they could. My parting message is not “Time heals all wounds” or “Everything happens for a reason” or “God only gives you what you can handle.” Quite the contrary: It makes no sense. You might have trouble coping at first. You might still feel emotional intrusions years later. At the same time, you, as a human, are inherently capable of holding two seemingly conflicting truths at the same time. I lost my family, yet I survived. It makes no sense, yet at the same time, it makes perfect sense.

item.title: How We Heal With Horses
item.description:
Therapy

How We Heal With Horses

After dealing with dark minds, I seek equine attunement.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Horses' innate environmental sensitivity offers benefits for those who gain their trust.
  • Multiple types of therapeutic programs employ them.
  • Besides hippotherapy, a horse can just be a friend.
Source: Credit: Greg Solderitch

I’ve been giving talks lately about the research I’ve done over the past 30 years on serial killers. At the end, I take questions. Generally, people ask how I deal with so much immersion in the vile things some people do. My response is that I do volunteer work on a horse farm. This puzzles people, but the healing effect of horses is well researched.

The most popular image of hippotherapy is the use of horses for special needs kids, especially those on the autism spectrum. I’ve witnessed its benefits. I once encouraged my undergraduate psychology students to apply for internships in a local equine therapy program, and we all saw how well the kids responded. The horse’s rhythmic motion had a soothing effect, and staying balanced brought confidence, but more important was the bonding experience. These kids were often isolated at school. The horses became their friends.

Theresa Williams, a licensed professional counselor at Red Horse Healing in South Dakota, has used horses in her practice for more than 15 years. She said the treatment brings comfort and mutual understanding. “Horses hear what is not spoken. They help create and maintain non-judgmental relationships.”

Therapy for Stress and Self-Regulation

Hippotherapy is a therapeutic modality; several U.S. therapy organizations offer certification, including the Equine Assisted Growth and Learning Association. The National Association of Social Workers, along with numerous college programs, supports its use. Multiple research publications found that equine-assisted interventions can reduce stress, lower cortisol levels, and improve self-regulation. I even saw it recommended for older people to help delay cognitive decline. Military veterans use it for treating PTSD.

For me, I have found mutual trust, mindfulness, and care. For the past four years, I’ve worked with a Kentucky Mountain Saddler named Sunny. He had his own needs, having been through laminitis and serious hoof surgery; assisting him back to soundness focused me fully on him. There wasn't any room for thinking about serial killers. In the process, I gained my own emotional and physiological benefits.

Because horses are prey animals, they're highly attuned to their environment, including to anyone who approaches them. They watch body language, listen to tone of voice, and even heart rate. If I’m nervous or moody, they’ll pick up on that. If I’m calm, they can relax and trust me. And their calmness draws me into a similar state. Their heartbeat attunes to mine. Each horse I encounter has a personality, a backstory, and a way of interacting. Trust is thus a process of negotiation. Once earned, it’s heartwarming—nothing beats hearing a nicker of recognition and welcome.

Addiction Recovery Through Horse Care

Other program types benefit from human-to-horse interaction, like those that help people trying to overcome addiction and rebuild their lives. They are built on the belief that recovery requires accountability, structure, and discipline. Healing through hands-on work like daily chores includes feeding, grooming, picking hooves, cleaning and bedding stalls, checking for injury, and learning about horse anatomy and vet care. The routine and structure help, but more important is the sense of partnership they can build with the horses in their care. It's a commitment.

My professional work takes an emotional toll, but time with horses heals me. It’s not just about being outside in the fresh air. It’s not just about riding. It’s mostly about connection with an intuitive animal that needs me to be present, focused, and protective. If I do that, I get more than enough back to keep my life balanced.

item.title: Why Victims Return to Abusers—and How to Explain It in Court
item.description:
Domestic Violence

Why Victims Return to Abusers—and How to Explain It in Court

A practical framework for recording how perpetrators use love to exert control.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Weaponized attachment is a pattern of perpetrator behaviour, not a disorder or pathology within the victim.
  • Perpetrators may use affection, withdrawal, and promises of repair to restrict a victim’s freedom.
  • Documentation should connect behaviour, attachment tactics, impact, and supporting evidence.

When a domestic abuse case reaches a courtroom, attention is often drawn to evidence that can be easily observed: a bruise, a threatening message, a 999 call, a weapon. Physical harm is relatively straightforward to document. It can be photographed, timestamped, measured, and presented to a jury.

Yet many victims experience forms of abuse that leave no visible injury. They may be monitored, isolated, degraded, manipulated, abandoned, intimidated, or controlled in ways that cannot be photographed, medically recorded, or easily measured (Stark & Hester, 2019). This creates a challenge for the court, because the harm may not appear as a single dramatic incident but as a pattern of behaviour that gradually restricts the victim’s freedom, alters their choices, and shapes how they respond to the perpetrator. In these cases, the task is to understand the pattern of control and its impact over time.

Perpetrator behaviours associated with coercive control, including weaponised attachment, can shape how victims think, feel, and behave. Victims adapt to survive within the relationship, and those adaptations are often misunderstood. They may send affectionate messages to the person who just hurt them. They may drop charges, defend the perpetrator to police, or return after separation. They may struggle to explain, even to themselves, why they are still there. These behaviours are routinely misread as irrationality, weakness, or consent when they may instead reflect the effects of a deliberate strategy employed by the perpetrator, in which the natural human need for love, connection, and belonging is weaponised against the victim.

When writing a case formulation, as a professional you should show two things:

  1. First, the formulation should explain how the perpetrator’s pattern of coercive and controlling behaviour affected the victim. This means looking beyond isolated incidents and identifying the repeated behaviours that shaped the victim’s choices, emotions, perceptions, and ability to leave or resist. This includes weaponised attachment, where the perpetrator uses affection, guilt, withdrawal, promises, threats, emotional dependence, or intermittent repair to maintain control. The focus should be on how the perpetrator’s behaviour created pressure, confusion, fear, hope, dependency, or compliance.
  2. Second, the formulation should set out the relationship history chronologically. It should show what the perpetrator did, when it happened, how often it occurred, how the pattern escalated or changed, and how the victim responded over time. This allows the court to understand behaviours that may otherwise appear contradictory, such as returning to the perpetrator, apologising, defending them, delaying separation, minimising harm, or maintaining contact. These responses should not be treated in isolation as evidence that the abuse was not serious. They may instead be evidence of the psychological and behavioural impact of coercive control and weaponised attachment.

What Is the Difference Between Love and Weaponised Attachment?

In healthy relationships, attachment promotes safety, trust, and mutual support. In coercive relationships, attachment can become a mechanism of domination. I explain this in more detail here.

Decades of research in psychology and neuroscience suggest that close relationships affect how people interpret threats, evaluate risks, experience distress, and pursue goals. Attachment is one of the primary ways through which people navigate the world.

The influence of attachment on behaviour is well established. Throughout history, people have endured hardship, taken extraordinary risks, and even sacrificed their lives for those they loved. Love changes behaviour because it changes affect. It shapes what people fear, what they hope for, what they attend to, and what they are willing to tolerate. The well-being of an attachment figure can become deeply intertwined with one's own emotional state.

Things to Document

Record four connected areas: perpetrator behaviour, the attachment mechanism, the impact on the victim, and supporting evidence. Arrange incidents chronologically to show how the pattern developed. See the table below as an example.

Table 1. Case Formulation Matrix for Documenting Weaponised Attachment and Coercive Control (Lesiak, 2026)
Source: Lesiak

1. Pattern of Perpetrator Behaviour

Describe specific actions and their sequence, including:

  • Intense affection followed by cruelty, humiliation, or withdrawal.
  • Apologies, gifts or promises of a shared future following abuse.
  • Threats of abandonment or replacement when the victim resists.
  • Claims that the perpetrator cannot cope or survive without the victim.
  • Demands that the victim demonstrate love through obedience, secrecy, or continued contact.
  • Appeals to children or family unity alongside pressure to reconcile.
  • Repeated crises that draw the victim back into contact.

Record what happened, when, how often, and what preceded or followed it. Include changes in the pattern and occasions when the victim resisted or sought support.

Specific descriptions are more useful than labels. “He stopped responding for three days after she refused to cancel a visit to her sister” conveys more than “He was emotionally manipulative.”

2. Attachment Mechanism

Explain how the behaviour operated through the emotional bond. Relevant questions include:

  • Was affection or reconciliation made conditional on compliance?
  • Did withdrawal create pressure to apologise, concede, or re-establish contact?
  • Did the perpetrator make the victim feel uniquely responsible for their well-being?
  • Were repeated promises of change used when the victim tried to leave?
  • Were harmful demands presented as expressions of love, vulnerability, or commitment?
  • Were attachments to children, pets, or family life used to pressure the victim?

Be clear about the connection. Financial pressure, monitoring, or threats may form part of coercive control, but their role in weaponised attachment needs explanation.

3. Impact on the Victim

Document how the pattern affected the victim’s choices, emotional life, and everyday activities. Relevant changes may include:

  • Delaying separation or returning after promises of change.
  • Withdrawing a complaint or withholding information from professionals.
  • Feeling responsible for preventing the perpetrator’s distress.
  • Reducing contact with friends, relatives, or support services.
  • Changing routines or avoiding disagreement to prevent retaliation.
  • Agreeing to arrangements because of guilt, fear, or pressure to preserve the family.

Ask what the response meant to the victim. An affectionate message might express continuing love, an attempt to calm the perpetrator, fear of abandonment, or several things at once. Avoid assigning a single explanation without exploring the circumstances.

4. Supporting Evidence

Identify material that helps establish the sequence and its effects, such as:

  • Messages, emails, voice notes, and call logs.
  • Threats followed by affection, apologies, or promises.
  • Communications making reconciliation conditional on particular actions.
  • Financial or housing records where these connect to the documented pressure.

Preserve the context of communications, including dates and surrounding exchanges. Identify who supplied each item and whether the practitioner reviewed it directly.

Writing the Summary

A summary should bring the documented pattern together and explain the basis for the interpretation. For example:

“Between [dates], the victim reported a repeated pattern of [specific behaviour], supported by [identified material]. She described responding by [actions] because she feared or hoped [her explanation]. The sequence suggests that affection, withdrawal, and promises of repair were used to influence her choices. This pattern may help explain her continued contact or apparent ambivalence within the wider account of coercive control.”

The central question is: How did the perpetrator create, intensify, or exploit the emotional bond, and how did that affect the victim’s freedom?

item.title: The Negative Impacts of Financial Illiteracy in the United States
item.description:
Education

The Negative Impacts of Financial Illiteracy in the United States

How we might improve financial literacy.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Decreased financial literacy may be related to our mostly cash-less society.
  • Financial literacy has been shown to be associated with improved financial outcomes.
  • Financial difficulties arising from financial illiteracy may lead to poorer mental health.
Source: Media Photos / Shutterstock

The ability to understand and effectively use financial skills among younger American adults appears to have declined over more than a decade.

For instance, on a standard five-question quiz about financial knowledge, adults ages 18–29 averaged 2.5 correct answers in 2009 but only 1.8 in 2021 (Urban & Valdes, 2022).

I believe that one of the reasons for this decreased financial literacy may be related to the absence of cash in our current-day society. Many children no longer see their parents counting out bills or change in stores.

Further, when purchases are made with credit or debit cards, and earnings and bills are handled by parents outside of their children’s awareness, children gain little exposure to how money is accumulated or used.

Without financial literacy, how can we expect young people to thrive without the need for assistance from their families, aid agencies, or the government?

Financial literacy has been shown to be associated with improved financial outcomes (Angrisani et al., 2023). Further, it is well recognized that financial difficulties, some of which can develop because of financial illiteracy, are associated with poorer physical and mental health, particularly depression (Samuel et al., 2025; Tibbetts et al., 2025).

In a 2023 Pew Research Center survey poll, American adults ages 50 and older (63 percent) were more likely than those 18 to 49 (45 percent) to say they were knowledgeable about personal finances.

Distressingly, only half of 18- to 29-year-olds were confident in their ability to create a monthly budget, a plan to pay off debt, or to save money.

Among U.S. adults who were knowledgeable about personal finances in this poll, 49 percent said they learned a great deal or a fair amount about personal finances from family and friends; 33 percent learned from the internet, 27 percent from their college, 24 percent from media including books, and only 19 percent from elementary or secondary schools.

Addressing Financial Illiteracy

I believe that financial illiteracy in the United States would be best addressed in high school (Brown et al., 2014). The families of young adults who are financially illiterate likely also have insufficient knowledge about personal finance (Kristoffersen & Gerrans, 2026).

Further, I believe that people who are financially illiterate are less likely to be able to glean appropriate financial information from the internet or media.

However, the American education system appears to have sidelined teaching personal finances to students for decades. Reasons for this deficit include:

  • Schools often focus on teaching standardized testing subject matters that may leave little room for other curricula such as classes about financial literacy (Mulhern et al., 2024; 220 Youth Leadership, 2025).
  • In 2009, less than one in five K-12 teachers said they felt very competent to teach personal finance (Way & Holden, 2009).
  • Cultural discomfort exists within American society around talking about finances (Empower, 2023). I believe one reason for this discomfort in schools may be related to inequalities in America related to financial literacy and financial means.

What About Our Politicians?

Given our poor track record with financial education, I wondered whether all our elected representatives who make budget decisions for our cities, counties, states, and nation have a good foundation in understanding finances.

I could find no study that assessed the knowledge of elected officials to answer my question.

Given the budgetary difficulties we are experiencing at all levels of government, I propose that our elected representatives be encouraged to:

  • Report as part of their campaigns their level of education and experience that is consistent with good financial literacy, including personal finance and public budget competence.
  • Assess their financial literacy upon assuming office. If necessary, they can be offered education to improve their financial knowledge base.

The Start of a Solution for Our Society

In the most recent decade, there has been a substantial increase in confidence from teachers in their ability to teach finances, largely thanks to new resources and training programs (Jorgensen, 2025).

To keep that momentum going, American citizens need to continue pressuring policymakers toward positive change. The education system can partner with financial education providers, like Junior Achievement USA and FitMoney, which provide free financial literacy materials (Field, 2020; Jorgensen, 2025).

Specific educational goals for a high-school financial-literacy curriculum could include learning about:

  • Budgeting, incorporating discussions about income, expenses, and discretionary spending.
  • Banking, interest, inflation, and compound growth.
  • Credit cards, credit scores, loans, and the risks of high-interest debt.
  • Saving for emergencies and longer-term goals.
  • Taxes, insurance, retirement accounts, and employee benefits.
  • Recognizing financial scams and evaluating online financial advice.

Students should have opportunities to construct a budget, compare loan offers, calculate the long-term cost of borrowing, and decide how to allocate a hypothetical paycheck, including through use of computer simulations to present real-world scenarios (Intuit Blog team, 2026).

Adults can involve children in age-appropriate discussions of household expenses, savings goals, and purchasing decisions. These conversations can be held without disclosure of private financial information.

Takeaway

Financial literacy cannot eliminate poverty or prevent every financial crisis. However, it can help individuals and our political representatives make informed decisions, recognize financial risks, manage debt, and plan for future expenses.

Also, because financial strain is associated with poorer mental and physical health, improving access to financial education is a worthwhile public health goal.

item.title: Is Our Current Approach to Mental Health in America Broken?
item.description:
Psychiatry

Is Our Current Approach to Mental Health in America Broken?

What goes wrong with the treatment of patients like Lindsay Clancy?

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • There is an underlying philosophy of psychiatry and psychology that informs our mental health system.
  • Accurate psychiatric diagnosis is essential to appropriate treatment.
  • Denial or naivete regarding the human capacity for evil is problematical and dangerous.
Lindsay Clancy
Source: Plymouth Superior Court, Public Domain, Wikimedia Commons

There has been much criticism of our current mental health system here in the United States and assignment of blame in the Lindsay Clancy case. As a clinician who has worked in and been part of that system both directly and indirectly, from both within and without it, for the past fifty years, I offer some reflections on what works and what doesn't work in such cases, and why.

How was Lindsay Clancy Treated by her Providers?

Ms. Clancy was a professional nurse and fairly high functioning member of society prior to the insidious decline of her mental health that led to strangling her three young children and then trying to kill herself. What triggered this horrific chain of events and why didn't she receive sufficient mental health support to prevent this evil deed from happening? Was this, as some assert, an abysmal failure of the mental health system as it currently exists here in America? Did Ms. Clancy never receive the level of psychiatric treatment clinically called for by the reported severity of her symptoms? Is this a common occurrence with other patients as well? Patients who simply "slip through the cracks" of a broken system? Was she somehow discriminated against because of her gender, as some allege? What, in retrospect, should her treatment have been? And why was it not provided? The benefit of 20-20 hindsight is, as always, a key factor here but nevertheless begs the question of why the mental health professionals Clancy consulted failed to recognize the severe risks that her concerning symptomatology posed. Or, if they did, why wasn't more done to try to prevent this tragedy from happening?

What Actually Went Wrong?

Following the birth of her third child, Ms. Clancy felt more anxious and overwhelmed, reportedly consulted two different psychiatrists, was diagnosed with an anxiety disorder, and promptly prescribed numerous psychiatric medications to mitigate her symptoms. To begin with, this begs the question of whether she was properly diagnosed at that time. In this sense, I disagree with fellow PT blogger Dr. Helen Marlo regarding the importance of preliminary psychiatric diagnosis which, in my view, is absolutely essential.

Correctly and quickly diagnosing such conditions is a crucial starting point for both effective pharmacological and psychological therapy. For example, diagnosing and treating an anxiety or adjustment disorder is very different from diagnosing and treating a bipolar, major depressive, borderline, or psychotic disorder. One challenge to diagnosing patients properly is that, because psychiatric symptoms, unlike objective signs (see my prior post) are subjective phenomena, unless one specifically asks about them, the person may not voluntarily report suicidal or homicidal ideation, hallucinations, or paranoia, etc. due to shame, fear of being judged, hospitalized, or perceived as being "crazy." And, even when directly asked, may deny having such symptoms. Were Ms. Clancy's symptoms never fully reported to the clinicians she consulted or merely missed, minimized, or overlooked by them? Were their diagnostic skills lacking? Or, was the potential dangerousness or her symptoms grossly underestimated?

The Underlying Philosophy of Mental Health Treatment Today

These are complex questions without easy answers. But I will attempt to address some of them here. Though we are speaking about the American mental health system in general, this case raises universal questions regarding the state of mental health care today. Modern psychiatry, psychology, and other mental health disciplines stand, whether they acknowledge it or not, upon certain fundamental philosophical beliefs regarding the nature of the human condition, the root causes of psychiatric symptoms and aberrant human behavior, the sources of human evil, violence, cruelty, and suffering, and the most effective and appropriate approaches for addressing these matters.

Indeed, the entire edifice of our mental health treatment system in this country is constructed upon these preconceived philosophical foundations which directly and indirectly, consciously and unconsciously, inform and influence how we conceptualize and treat mental health issues. So, we could say that what happened to Ms. Clancy and, unfortunately, happens to many others seeking psychiatric or psychological assistance today, can be attributed to a fallacious philosophy underlying the mental health system. But how so?

The predominant philosophical misconception of mainstream psychiatric and psychological treatment today is that since so-called mental disorders are presumed to be primarily neurobiological phenomena, their main treatment must be biological or biochemical. Moreover, that pharmacological intervention is both faster, cheaper, and more efficacious than psychotherapy in alleviating the patient's symptoms and suffering, and that this is the only purpose of treatment. (See my prior posts.) Additionally, that CBT, DBT, and other brief or short-term therapies are superior to more open-ended approaches such as psychodynamic, existential, or humanistic therapies. CBT (cognitive-behavioral therapy) or DBT (dialectical behavior therapy) might be better for addressing and mitigating certain specific symptoms or behaviors but not others. And brief therapy can be sufficient in some cases, but certainly not all, or even most. When critical treatment decisions are made on the basis of dogmatic clinical philosophy, not to mention financial considerations, the consequences will be predictably disastrous.

Moreover, most seasoned psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, and other mental health professionals recognize, at least to some extent, the inherent dangers of certain archetypal kinds of symptom patterns, as well as the congenital human capacity for evil or destructive behavior toward self or others, and take aggressive steps to mitigate these dangers whenever possible, whether that involves voluntary or involuntary hospitalization, more intensive outpatient treatment, etc. Why did this not happen here?

For instance, in December, 2022, Ms. Clancy eventually sought outpatient psychiatric treatment at the Women and Infants Hospital Center for Women's Behavioral Health, a clinical setting specializing in perinatal and postpartum care and presumably sensitive and highly attuned to women's mental health issues in particular, but was supposedly told there that she was not suffering from postpartum depression, let alone postpartum psychosis. Yet, according to her husband, she expressed suicidal ideation and thoughts of harming her children to him at that time. So, this catastrophic failure of the system is not necessarily about gender, but, rather, about clinical naivete, i.e., the refusal or failure to recognize and take seriously the risks of her alarming symptomatology and the potentiality for evil or destructive, violent behavior.

Denial of the very real human capacity for evil is an exceedingly dangerous defense mechanism in mental health professionals. Failure or refusal to foresee and attempt to prevent the possible worse scenarios or outcomes in such cases, can itself be catastrophic. The unwillingness to acknowledge the patient's human capacity for evil curtails the clinician's ability to intervene aggressively and prophylactically when needed.

Could This Act Have Been Deterred?

Had Clancy been admitted to and participated in an intensive treatment program or been urged to continue to attend ongoing psychotherapy sessions, she could have been much more closely monitored for any changes in or exacerbation of her fragile psychiatric condition. Here I concur completely with my colleague Dr. Marlo's point regarding the necessity and benefits of psychodynamic or other more intensive longer-term outpatient therapies in such cases and that being in a more open-ended therapy on at least a weekly basis could have potentially reduced the chances of this tragic crime occurring. However, having said that, the sad reality is that even when patients suffering from severe and dangerous symptoms such as command hallucinations, paranoid delusions, suicidal or homicidal ideation, and profound depression or anxiety are regularly seeing a psychotherapist or psychiatrist, the outcome is not necessarily always good. Some evil deeds are not always preventable.

item.title: How to Relieve the Stress of Judgment
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

How to Relieve the Stress of Judgment

6 steps to taking control of your reactive brain.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • To protect us, our brains are always judging situations. We can't stop judging but we can stop reacting.
  • Start controlling your mind by learning how your body signals it is having an emotional reaction.
  • Creating the habit of exercising emotional choice requires diligent practice and self-compassion.
Source: VitalikRadko / depositphotos

Every day I read articles and posts about the growing divisiveness in the world. It is difficult to have a conversation with anyone whose opinions differ from our own.

Not only are we becoming increasingly judgmental, but our quickness to disrespectfully react with ridicule or contempt is also damaging our relationships and our health. Judgment triggers tension. Your breathing quickens. Your heart and blood pressure rise. Your face flushes, your thoughts narrow, and you feel a jolt of self-protection. Your reaction might range from a mumbled cynical remark to a personal attack on the speaker’s intelligence.

However, biting your tongue so you don't say anything is still harmful. The stress from suppressing negative reactions can weaken the immune system, strain your cardiac and digestive systems, and affect your sleep.1

It’s also likely people will feel the energy of your negative emotions even if you have mastered keeping your face blank. Small gestures, like pursing your lips or looking at your hands, might indicate your displeasure with what was said.

The impact of your reactions can damage trust and adversely affect the outcome of your conversations. You might shame people into compliant silence, or they resentfully, and often with a louder tone, explain themselves, which could increase your judgmental reaction.

Why we are judgmental

We are all judgmental by nature. Anyone who says they don’t judge just isn’t aware of when they do. You may be less critical than others you know, but you can’t help being biased and judgmental.2 The brain’s primary job is to keep you safe. For survival, your brain needs to recognize situations that can be hurtful because sometimes they are.

The brain is always judging if situations are good or bad, right or wrong before you can determine if your brain is wrong or, at least, not helpful.

Your brain is reactive, but you have the power to override your judgment by first noticing your judgment as an emotional reaction. Emotional awareness frees you to choose what you want to feel instead.3 You probably will never be free of judgmental reactions, but you don’t have to be the victim of these responses. With practice, you can decrease both the frequency and amplitude of your reactions.

Practicing emotional choice

  1. Familiarize yourself with how your body signals your emotional reactions. Do you feel it in your stomach, shoulders, chest, sweaty palms, or somewhere else? You might feel tightness in your jaw or your toes.
  2. Notice what habitually triggers your judgment. If you track your emotional states during the day, you can better define situations and behaviors that trigger strong judgmental reactions. Use this emotional inventory to help you monitor your emotions and moods for two to three weeks. This will help you develop your self-awareness.
  3. Look for patterns. You might find you are more vulnerable in specific situations or time periods when you are tired or hungry. This awareness can help you prepare for difficult conversations and better regulate your emotional state.
  4. Choose another emotion to embody. What would you rather feel instead of judgment? Do you want to feel calm, compassionate, or curious? Maybe you can shift to being amused if the subject is not that important? Before you go into a conversation, pick one emotional state you want to maintain. When you notice your judgment arising, think of the one emotion you want to feel instead and breathe it into your body to help you shift your emotions to this state.
  5. Celebrate your wins at the end of each day. The brain needs evidence of success before it will work with you to change your habits. Instead of beating yourself up for being reactive, make note of the times you were able to decrease your impatience or you set a boundary around conversation topics to maintain positive connections. Find a meaningful way to celebrate your wins so your brain seeks this reward and supports your growth.
  6. Be diligent with your practice, and forgive yourself when you slip. Habits take time to both embed and outweigh old habits. New habits require continual application until they become the natural way of responding. Because of the brain’s insistence on protecting you, you will relapse and act judgmentally. Remember you are human, then keep practicing.

Bonus tip: Eat and sleep well. Your patience is impaired by sleep deprivation, poor nutrition, noise pollution, excessive conflict, money problems, and a shortage of friends.

Your ability to remain in control of your judgmental reactions is your power to manage your stress and maintain healthy relationships.

item.title: How to Compromise With Purpose
item.description:
Mindfulness

How to Compromise With Purpose

What the artistic process teaches us about embracing complexity.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Music can help us cultivate mindful awareness to find more agency.
  • Compromising is essential in composing a meaningful life.
  • Allow multiple responses to unfold over time.

The word “compromise” often carries a negative connotation in our assertive society. Yet it actually contains two meanings: one being less than it was, and the other being the art of navigating and negotiating the best way forward. This fascinating word was the inspiration behind my recent Classical Music Explorations performance, and the artistic process gave me new insights into how I can upgrade the way I process life situations.

Cultivate Musical Mindfulness to Find More Agency

How well we use our innate gifts of curiosity, consciousness, and creativity to find a compromise in times of constraint is not a matter of luck but the fruit of a consistent cultivation of skills. When we regularly listen to music that was written as a conscious communication, a part of the humanities, we become more adept at finding multiple points of engagement with each life circumstance.

Contrary to the instant results promised by consumerism, lasting mindfulness takes a long time to develop. It changes the person, not just the circumstance. In psychology, this may be called cognitive restructuring. In religion, spiritual formation. In piano skills, proficiency and artistry. In composition, craftsmanship. In a relationship, emotional maturity. These fruits come from efforts to compromise one's current desires for a greater good.

Compromising Is Essential in Composing a Meaningful Life

One of the greatest threats to our survival—in this age of entangled communications and complex systems—is our rigidity in not accepting anything less than our ideals. It may sound heroic in a storybook, but in modern life, not compromising can lead to acting against one’s own interests and letting a single issue create a blind spot in the bigger reality.

Our ability to find self-awareness and our agency to act on it will determine our ability to maintain relationships, family units, a nation, and even our existence as a species on this planet. In this world, we find compromise in thorny issues that are “49/51”—full of complexity. (This is referencing the TV show "The Diplomat," season 1, among other sources.) Moving forward depends on choosing a lesser evil when we can’t have an ideal choice.

Allow Multiple Responses to Unfold Over Time

Attending to concert music can be an artistic process if we are discovering layers and angles as the music unfolds. We find the compromise of what to focus on among a multitude of stimuli.

As I grappled with the topic of "The Compromise of Space," which was also the name of my performance involving three favorite pieces, I discovered three choices of action when I feel compromised, compressed, or constrained.

  • Option 1: Share my space (Bach-Siloti: "Prelude in B minor"): In music, a composer can diminish the distance between notes in a chord (vertical grouping of notes) to express compression. In times of sorrow, we feel constrained in what we are able to do. But at the same time, we are more likely to let go of masks and expectations, which is required for bonding and sharing our space with others. The sense of camaraderie formed in authentic vulnerability is much stronger than the bonds formed between “fine-weather friends.” (This phrase refers to Lucy Maud Montgomery’s beloved book Anne of Green Gables.)
  • Option 2: Claim my space (Brandon Vaccaro: "Insomnia"): In music, when the composer uses harmony or textures to build tension, the release might not be a resolution but a sudden change in direction with a new chord, or the entrance of a new melody. It is a call to action, a way to claim the moment. The climax is just as much a psychological revelation that something is possible as any actual physical change. With insomnia, we can claim our moment and space in a literal way by going to a different room or deciding to stay awake for a while.
  • Option 3: Find more space (Schubert-Liszt: "Du Bist die Ruh"): In music, creating sweep and scope requires a performer to use breath and imagination, two elements that are equally important for responding in real time to real life.

Try One of These 1-Minute Exercises

  1. Look up into eternity and infinity, or to the farthest and highest corner of your room. Include your peripheral vision. It helps to start at a physically expansive environment like a concert hall or an outdoor park. Can you let your guard down so you can share this space?
  2. Vertically anchor in opposition with your feet down into the ground. Feel the natural heaviness of your tailbone. In opposition, lift the crown of your head while listening to your favorite music (in your head or on a device). Where is the peak of each phrase? Can you find a little extra space in your lungs to claim that moment?
  3. Horizontally expand your ribcage. Extend arms with air underneath, allowing the surrounding air to support you. Inhale horizontally across your ears, where numerous nerves are located. Where is the longest note of each phrase? Can you broaden your inhale to find more space? More ways to negotiate the best way forward?
