item.title: When Love Becomes a Refuge From Reality
item.description:
Relationships

When Love Becomes a Refuge From Reality

Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans are a stunning example of shared pathology.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • The concept of "folie à deux" involves two people sharing a delusional belief system.
  • This French term translates loosely to "madness for two" and became known as shared psychotic disorder.
  • Genuine intimacy allows two people to remain connected while recognizing each other as separate individuals.
  • Fusion, by contrast, can make acknowledging any differences feel intolerable.

In 1877, French psychiatrists Charles Lasègue and Jules Falret introduced the concept of folie à deux, a condition in which two people share a delusional belief system. The French term translates loosely to "madness for two" and eventually became known as shared psychotic disorder. Although it no longer exists as a standalone diagnosis in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5), the concept remains relevant to understanding how two people can reinforce a distorted perception of reality.

It also feels remarkably relevant while attempting to unpack Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's brilliant documentary, You Can See Everything, about Elizabeth Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans.

The film opens just over a month before Holmes is scheduled to begin a multi-year prison sentence for defrauding investors in Theranos, the blood-testing company she founded after dropping out of Stanford. Once celebrated as the world's youngest self-made female billionaire, Holmes now faces enormous financial liabilities and an 11-year prison sentence. Yet she remains adamant that she did absolutely nothing wrong.

Her devoted and bewildering partner, Billy Evans, wholeheartedly supports her version of events. Together, they invite Fielder into their home, apparently hoping to demonstrate both Holmes's innocence and, perhaps even more importantly, the extraordinary nature of their love.

The more directly Fielder confronts Holmes with uncomfortable questions, the clearer it becomes that the couple appears to inhabit a reality of their own construction. Any suggestion of wrongdoing is met with deflection, often giving way to elaborate descriptions or performances of their unusually profound mutual devotion. The self-described mythical nature of their love for one another seems to become a defense mechanism proving their innocence.

Fielder, known for his fascination with simulated realities in shows like The Rehearsal, seems particularly well suited to explore this psychological terrain. He is direct but nuanced. His questions are no-nonsense but he becomes deeply engaged. The harder he tries to understand Holmes and Evans, the more elusive their reality becomes.

What emerges is a portrait of two people who appear to have become lost in each other, using the intensity of their emotional connection as a refuge from the painful realities surrounding them. Their shared conviction in the extraordinary nature of both Holmes's professional mission and their romantic relationship seems to serve a powerful psychological purpose.

Holmes has been convicted of defrauding investors, yet Evans appears unwavering in his acceptance of her claims of complete innocence. Meanwhile, Evans engages in behavior that appears to violate Holmes's trust in ways that are difficult to comprehend. Yet she seems remarkably untroubled by these apparent betrayals.

Perhaps this is because acknowledging either partner's troubling behavior would threaten the emotional refuge they have constructed together. The grand nature of their love becomes an apt metaphor for the majestic mission of Theranos. Their devotion appears to depend, at least in part, on a mutual willingness to look away.

The Psychology of Distorted Relationship Patterns

From a psychological perspective, relationships develop their own equilibrium, and couples can become deeply invested in maintaining familiar patterns, even when those patterns distort their understanding of themselves and the world around them. For Holmes and Evans, their shared insistence on the exceptional nature of their love may serve to protect them from a myriad of painful truths.

Consider an important distinction between intimacy and fusion. Genuine intimacy allows two people to remain connected while recognizing each other as separate individuals, capable of mistakes, contradictions, and disappointments. Fusion, by contrast, can make acknowledging those differences feel intolerable. When a couple becomes emotionally fused, protecting the relationship can begin to take precedence over confronting reality.

The question is not whether Holmes and Evans meet the clinical criteria for a dual delusional disorder. The more relevant question is what it looks like when two people become so invested in protecting their emotional connection that acknowledging reality begins to feel like a threat to the relationship itself.

The very relationship that seems to offer them safety may also prevent them from inhabiting any semblance of reality.

We see everything and know nothing.

item.title: Can Creativity Be a Stress-Buster?
item.description:
Stress

Can Creativity Be a Stress-Buster?

Creative engagement can be a tool for managing stress.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • There seems to be a positive link between regular creative engagement and the reduction of stress.
  • Not all creative activities are psychologically beneficial for all people.
  • There are five easy-to-implement practices that can reduce your daily stressors.

Stress is an unavoidable part of daily life, whether it stems from work deadlines, family responsibilities, financial concerns, or overwhelming demands on our attention. But what if we could insert small doses of creativity into our everyday routines? A growing body of research suggests that regular engagement in creative activities may contribute to stress reduction and emotional well-being (although the effects vary from person to person). Let's explore some research and how we might put it into practice.

What the Research Says

A compelling 2024 study involved a cohort of college students who participated in a four-week art-making program that included freehand drawing, clay modeling, and crafts. Researchers used the Perceived Stress Scale to assess participants’ stress. Results indicated that the art-making group showed a significant reduction in perceived stress from before to after the intervention. Additionally, the researchers suggested that individuals don’t need to produce professional-quality artwork to help them manage everyday stress.

In a 2025 study, researchers conducted a 10-week randomized controlled trial involving 76 college students. Participants took part in a program featuring facilitated drumming and dancing. The researchers discovered significantly greater reductions in stress in the intervention group than in the control group at the conclusion of the program. They also emphasized that creativity isn’t just limited to writing and painting, but that music and rhythmic movements with others may also help people manage their stress. So too does musical engagement offer expanded opportunities for social interaction.

Another 2024 study evaluated a structured gallery-based program that encouraged participants to slow down and engage thoughtfully with art. Subsequently, participants reported a significant reduction in perceived stress one day after the intervention. So too did the researchers note improvements in mindfulness measures. This study focused on an appreciation of art rather than its creation. It seems to indicate evidence for the broader idea that intentional engagement with the arts can also provide a restorative break from daily pressures.

The research above, along with other studies, strongly suggests that creative engagement can be a viable tool for managing stress. That is, creativity can be accessible (drawing, painting, and drumming do not require advanced skills), the experience is more important than the finished product (participation is more critical than achievement), and different creative activities serve different purposes (making art, engaging in dancing sessions, and museum explorations are not identical interventions). What also becomes clear is that 1) additional studies are necessary, 2) not all creative activities reduce stress for everyone, and 3) creativity is not a simple substitute for professional care when stress becomes overwhelming.

Research Into Practice

Source: Tho-Ge/Pixabay

At this point, it seems reasonable to assume that some engagement in one or more creative activities has the potential to provide us with a healthy outlet for our emotions and an opportunity to redirect our attention away from worries. So too do activities such as art, music, and writing offer effective outlets for us to communicate feelings without the necessity of explanation. Equally important, creative activities may be an opportunity to make choices while restoring a feeling of agency. In sum, regular creative activities hold the potential of offering a calming alternative to tasks driven by deadlines, competition, or expectations. Let’s take a look at a few.

1. Time in Nature. Just taking a short walk in nature has been shown, via numerous studies, to reduce anxiety, calm emotions, and moderate our stress. Shifting our concentration to flowers, trees, meadows, forests, animals and the like is balm for both mind and body. Rachet this experience up a notch by using your phone to take photographs of beautiful gardens, interesting landscapes, dynamic skies, interesting animals, compelling shadows, or anything natural you find particularly beautiful. When you return home assemble a collection of photos into an ongoing journal or photo album to share with friends and colleagues.

2. Journaling. Writing is a natural way of organizing our thoughts, processing difficult experiences, and gaining perspective on troubling emotions. In writing, you assume control over the words you use to express yourself. Consider a daily activity (15 minutes) of emotional journaling—writing about whatever is on your mind: good, bad, or otherwise. The only audience is yourself, so don’t worry about grammar, spelling, or style—just write. Give yourself permission to review past writings every so often.

3. Drawing, Painting, Doodling. Take time off (e.g., 15 minutes) and spend it drawing, painting, or doodling. No artistic skill is necessary—just create whatever comes to mind. When you change your attention to the colors, shapes, and patterns of various types of subject matter you offer your mind an opportunity to refocus and reorient—rather than constantly thinking about stressful situations.

4. Making Music. One very powerful creative strategy that significantly improves our mood is our active engagement in music. Singing to yourself (even if off-key), singing along with one of your favorite artists, creating a tune out of thin air, or listening to some favorite tunes all have positive benefits for our psyche. Music invites us in and offers an opportunity to express our emotions, create a sense of enjoyment, or provide a social connection to others. So, sing your favorite song, play a musical instrument, or just tap a happy rhythm on your desk. A musical interlude is always beneficial.

5. Hands-On. Consider making one or more of the following a part of your day: knitting, sculpting clay, crocheting, building a model airplane, woodworking, pottery-making, embroidery, or gardening. These activities need not produce a finished product to be beneficial. The process itself—working with your hands, concentrating on a manageable task, and temporarily setting aside everyday concerns—may be an important part of their stress-relieving appeal.

Know that engagement in creative activities is not guaranteed to reduce stress for everyone. An activity that feels relaxing to one person might be frustrating for another. The key is to select activities you find to be particularly enjoyable—irrespective of whether or not you have any specific talent in that area. Simply put, you don’t have to be a professional artist, writer, or woodworker to benefit from creativity. You simply have to give yourself permission to create something meaningful (to you) without the worry of whether or not it’s good.

item.title: The Lives We Didn't Live: What-Ifs, Regret, and Marriage
item.description:
Identity

The Lives We Didn't Live: What-Ifs, Regret, and Marriage

Do you ever wonder who you'd be if you'd chosen differently?

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Counterfactual thinking can help eflect on past decisions, recognize unmet needs, and identify possibilities.
  • Valuing relationships doesn't mean we can't acknowledge personal ambitions or opportunities we've set aside.
  • We can use reflections of the past to make meaningful changes in the present.
Lori Loughlin and Tom Cavanagh
Source: Hallmark Media

As I approach my 50th birthday, I notice myself reflecting more on the what-ifs. What if I had chosen a different major, pursued another career, or moved to a different city? Who might I be now? These questions can feel scary or uncomfortable to ask, especially if different choices would impact our closest relationships. We may love the people in our lives and still reflect on a life we might have lived or wonder about the possibilities of different realities. Would we have been happier if we had chosen differently?

This tension is the focus of What If Christmas. This movie asks viewers to consider how minor or major decisions might have changed the direction of their lives. In other words, What If?

Erin (Lori Loughlin) has always supported the career of her husband, Adam (Tom Cavanagh), a heart surgeon. Each year, she organizes his hospital’s Christmas charity gala, which gives her a sense of accomplishment and purpose. When Adam moves to another hospital, however, Erin’s planning and expertise is no longer needed.

Without that role, she increasingly regrets having given up her career in fashion design to support Adam’s. She wonders what would have happened had she pursued her career ambitions instead of setting them aside for her marriage. Eventually, and after being gifted a magical ornament, she wakes up in an alternative reality where she is a successful fashion designer.

These alternate-reality plot-lines aren’t new to Hallmark. What If Christmas uses this premise, though, to explore the common midlife challenge of evaluating the life we’ve built and whether it still makes room for parts of ourselves that we value.

The Psychology of What If

Psychologists call the process of mentally constructing alternatives to events that have already happened counterfactual thinking. Sometimes, we may imagine how things could have turned out better. This is called upward counterfactual thinking. Erin’s belief that life would have been better if she pursued her career is one example. Other times, we imagine how things could have been worse. This is downward counterfactual thinking. Erin learning, through living in her alternative reality, that pursuing her career meant never meeting Adam would be an example.

Neither type of counterfactual thinking tells us what actually would have happened had we made a different choice. An imagined life remains in the imagination. We can harness the power of counterfactual thinking to help us, though. Through reflections on past decisions, we may learn from previous mistakes to make better decisions in the future. Positive counterfactual thinking is when our imagined reality helps us understand something new or take action. When counterfactual thinking keeps our imagined reality on constant replay without gaining a new perspective, it can lead to anxiety or depression.

Erin becomes increasingly caught in believing that pursuing fashion would have given her an ideal life. Evaluating a career path is not in itself problematic. Erin could have realized that she missed having an outlet to express her creativity instead of feeling like she needed a wholly different life. That realization could have inspired her to seek out opportunities for creativity in her actual reality.

Unless Santa gives us a magical ornament, our past remains the same no matter how much counterfactual thinking we do. What we learn from it, however, can help us change our present, perhaps for the better.

When a Familiar Role No Longer Fits

Developmental psychologist Erik Erikson theorized the central challenge of middle adulthood as generativity versus stagnation. Generativity involves caring for others and contributing, creating, and nurturing something that will outlast us. Parenting, mentoring, teaching, and community work can all provide opportunities for contribution.

Erin’s charitable work for the hospital provides an example of generativity. When that role disappears, she wonders where to direct her skills and care and questions her place in the world. It becomes clear to viewers that she valued supporting Adam’s career, but it’s also clear that her needs weren’t fully being met. These feelings are worth considering, and this movie encourages that type of reflection. What If Christmas leaves viewers with a weighty question: What might the life you didn’t choose reveal about the life you still have the opportunity to create?

What Is the Imagined Life Asking for?

When a particular what-if keeps returning, consider the following questions:

  1. What attracts me to this imagined life?
  2. Which part of it could I pursue now?
  3. What support or changes would it require?

We may be surprised to find that we don’t want an entirely different life. We may want to be more creative, to mentor future generations, to learn new skills, or to be more independent. Identifying the need beneath the fantasy gives us a specific pathway forward instead of a general wish to undo our present life. We can’t know who we would have become, but we can ask what those imagined possibilities reveal about the choices we can still make today.

Hallmark vs. Psychology

Hallmark says: A magical glimpse of an alternative life can reveal unmet needs in the present.

Psychology says: Imagining other outcomes can help us learn and plan. Its usefulness depends on whether we have a healthy balance between informative self-reflection and unhelpful rumination.

Verdict: Halllmark offers a useful starting point. We don’t need a magical ornament to explore an unmet need; we can evaluate our past and the impact it has on our present at any time of year.

Sometimes, we don't want a different life as much as we want to recover a part of ourselves that we've forgotten.

item.title: I Froze My Eggs, So Why Don’t I Feel Better?
item.description:
Infertility

I Froze My Eggs, So Why Don’t I Feel Better?

Egg freezing doesn't always bring relief or reassurance. Why?

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Egg freezing can preserve reproductive options, but it cannot guarantee a future pregnancy or live birth.
  • Egg freezing does not necessarily mean freedom from reproductive worries.
  • Understanding expectations may help better manage uncertainty afterwards.
Source: PeopleImages/Shutterstock

Egg freezing is presented as an empowering decision. A way of taking charge of your reproductive life, preserving your options and buying yourself a little more time. A chance to beat the clock. And for many women, that is precisely what happens. [1] But what happens psychologically after the eggs are frozen? This is an account of three women who underwent the same medical procedure, yet each had a very different psychological response.

When Relief Turns Into Disappointment

“At the time, when I froze my eggs, I felt relieved. I felt it was good self-care, I was being proactive and that it bought me some time. I can’t believe none of that is true now.” — MJ

One of the hardest things for MJ to reconcile was that her eggs did not survive the freeze-thaw process. She understood intellectually that egg freezing preserved reproductive potential rather than guaranteeing a baby. But that understanding was of little comfort when she discovered her eggs were no longer viable.

What struck me about MJ’s experience was not simply her disappointment with the medical outcome, but the loss of the psychological reassurance she had gained from freezing her eggs. It had felt like the responsible thing to do, allowing her to worry a little less about her reproductive future. When she discovered that her eggs had not survived thawing, she described feeling devastated, angry and incredibly anxious. It felt as though the rug had been pulled out from under her. In so many areas of our lives, taking action helps reduce uncertainty. We make plans, put safeguards in place and feel reassured that we have done what we can. But reproduction doesn’t always work that way. MJ had done what she could to preserve her fertility, yet the outcome was still beyond her control.

It wasn’t that she had done anything wrong, or that her eggs had somehow failed her. The science of egg freezing, despite how far it has come, still has its limitations. [4,5] And for MJ, those limitations had very real emotional consequences.

When Egg Freezing Creates More Anxiety

“It was really weird, I actually started to stress more about the whole thing. I thought freezing my eggs would bring relief, but it got worse! I worry if they really got enough, should I do it again as a safety measure, what about freeze-thaw? I don’t even know if there is a right or wrong place to stop.” — PG

PG’s experience was quite different. Before freezing her eggs, she worried about her age, whether she would meet the right partner, and whether she would have the opportunity to become a mother. She hoped egg freezing would quiet some of those worries. Instead, the object of her anxiety changed. Now she worried about the number of eggs she had frozen, whether they would survive thawing, whether they would fertilize, and whether she should undergo another retrieval, just in case. In other words, she had completed the medical procedure, but she didn’t feel psychologically finished.

This is something I see repeatedly in fertility treatment. We often imagine that reaching a particular medical milestone will bring psychological relief. But completing a medical procedure doesn’t necessarily mean the emotional uncertainty has been resolved. And while there may be sound medical reasons to consider another retrieval [4], there is also a psychological question worth considering:

Am I thinking about another cycle because it would meaningfully improve my reproductive options, or because I am hoping it will finally make me feel safe?

If what we really seek is certainty that everything will work out fine, there may never be a number of cycles that feels sufficient. The question then becomes how we live with that uncertainty. Sometimes we have to make decisions without knowing whether they are the right ones and learn to accept that we may never feel completely sure.

When Egg Freezing Doesn’t Change How You Feel

“I thought I’d feel more relieved, like I had done something. I actually don’t feel any different. I don’t even think about it.” — DD

DD’s response is interesting because it seems so uneventful. She had expected egg freezing to bring some emotional benefit—a sense of relief, accomplishment, and greater control over her reproductive future. Instead, she felt much the same. She was disappointed, having read about other women feeling empowered, liberated, and reassured by what was described as a meaningful form of self-care.

She had hoped her decision and emotions would line up, confirming that she had made the right choice. What she discovered was that she felt neutral, even after taking what felt like a big, worthwhile step. Psychologically, a neutral response is not a sign that something went wrong but maybe simply that the decision has settled into its proper place, as one sensible step rather than something that has to carry one's emotional future.

MJ, PG, and DD all went into the process of egg freezing with the same idea: to preserve their reproductive options and buy some time. Yet their emotional responses differed greatly, raising the question: What are we hoping egg freezing will do for us emotionally?

Sometimes we unconsciously give those eggs a much bigger job: to reassure us that motherhood will still be available when we are ready, or to allow us to stop thinking about fertility and regret. That’s a lot to ask of a collection of cells sitting in a laboratory freezer. And it could partly explain why psychological responses to egg freezing are so varied. Understanding what we are asking of egg freezing psychologically may help us recognise the kind of support we need, both during the process and afterwards.

Preserving Options Is Not the Same as Securing Outcomes

It’s important to remember that egg freezing can preserve reproductive options, but it cannot secure a reproductive outcome. Long-term research shows that many women who freeze their eggs never return to use them—and that for those who do, a live birth is by no means guaranteed. [3,4]

Frozen eggs preserve possibility, but possibility and certainty are not the same thing. If we expect egg freezing to provide both, even a medically successful retrieval may leave us feeling strangely unfinished.

Research has found that many women are satisfied with their decision to freeze their eggs, although some experience regret. [2,6] But satisfaction and relief are not the same thing. You can think, I’m glad I froze my eggs, and still feel, I’m worried about whether I will be able to have a child. In the end, perhaps one can only aspire to feel comfortable with the thought, I have given myself the very best opportunity in a situation that isn't entirely in my hands.

item.title: A Conversation With a New Mom
item.description:
Career

A Conversation With a New Mom

Let’s listen with a third ear to what new moms are saying.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • New moms' honest stories reveal the unfiltered roller coaster of early motherhood.
  • Sudden medical issues can upend birth plans and force unexpected emotional adjustments.
  • Maternal intuition—like Kim’s attention to her itch—can be life-saving and should be trusted.

We need to listen to the stories of new moms and applaud those who can talk about their life in the midst of their pre- and post-birth fuzziness and glow.

It’s so true that we often forget the last days of pregnancy and the first days of motherhood when we are in a daze. Those are important moments that need to be remembered. The problem is what we lose in the forgetting.

We need to move from our focus on the traditional birth plan and ideals about the fourth trimester to a space where questioning, curiosity, and the contradictory feelings about mothering can be fostered as a core part of mothering.

A Real-Life Story of Transition to Motherhood

A childhood friend of my daughter’s, let’s call her Kim, recalls so eloquently what we'll call the rocky transition into motherhood. She sent me a message that her baby had been born a little early, but they were good. When I talked to my daughter, she warned me not to visit Kim. She said she had a hard time. I was curious about what my daughter meant.

I sent Kim a few texts and an important conversation followed.

Kim gave me permission to write her story, her truth.

She told me no one had told her about what mothering was really like. This is the catchcry of my work.

Kim’s story went something like this:

She was due to give birth mid-October. She had it all worked out. She would leave her high-powered job that she loved on Friday, Sept 25. This would give her time to do her handover at work and two weeks at home to mentally and physically prepare for the birth, to nest. She was looking forward to this hiatus as an opportunity to get the nursery ready and to spend some time with her husband before the baby came and they would become a family of three.

In the week leading up to her last day at work, she started to develop an itch. She didn’t think much about it until her sister, a doctor, told her it might indicate a liver condition and she insisted that she have it checked.

The itch was getting worse so on the Thursday, Kim made an appointment to see the doctor who was covering for her obstetrician who was away. He could only see her at 1 p.m., which clashed with a crucial and final handover meeting at work. She decided that her baby’s health comes first. Mother’s intuition. The doctor agreed with her sister’s diagnosis of cholestasis, a serious liver condition for the baby. Kim was advised that her safest option was to deliver her baby on Monday morning.

Kim was in shock. She was very worried about her baby and upset that her own doctor wouldn't be there for the birth. She felt that she had no time to prepare. Her last day of work was hectic and she wasn't close enough to anyone at work to confide in about her situation.

Her weekend was a complete haze for her.

The baby was born on Monday. All went well. But I suspected this wasn’t the whole story. Over the next weeks, Kim sent me texts that were honest and raw and illustrate the roller coaster of new motherhood.

The First Days as a New Mom

On Tuesday she texted me, “It hasn't hit me yet. I’m going to read your book during my maternity leave."

“My last day of work was only on Friday. It’s been madness, I finally feel like myself”

“This baby doesn't even look like me”

“It’s wild I still don’t even recognise myself. But every day I love her more and more. At first I was like ‘who is this alien?’”

“My husband and I are completely in love. She is ‘the sweetest’”

On Wednesday: “It’s been a major adjustment."

“I was pooped on everywhere last night at 3 a.m. [with a laughing emoji]. Just like a full explosion”

“Thankfully all I do is feed and sleep. My husband does everything else that needs to be done.”

“It’s an absolute shock to the body. Adjusting to these feeding windows every three hours without much sleep. But she’s such a cute little mouse”

Key Takeaways From Kim's Experience

What this story reinforces for me:

  • The importance of a mother owning and telling her unique birth story. The recognition that any traumatic birth experiences, like Kim’s health scare or an unexpected early delivery, require special care and oversight.
  • A new mom’s identity is necessarily in free-fall and involves recalibration. A baby has its own timeline, which requires a mother’s total surrender and change in priorities. Kim needed to make the sudden shift from pregnancy to being a mom without her desired time to nest. Becoming a mom is a shock in so many different ways. This needs to be recognized, articulated, and normalised as part of mothering.
  • A new mom’s voice is valuable. It needs to be respected, claimed and listened to. A new mom knows herself. In this case, Kim listened to her body and her intuition. Her itch meant something. Kim mentioned to me that expectant mother’s need to know about the danger of cholestasis.
  • A new mom who is surrounded by a loving and supportive network has the best chance for a smooth transition into, and experience of, mothering. Kim has a husband who looks after her while she cares for the baby, a father and two sisters, who have also had babies in the last two months, and close in-laws. She realizes how fortunate she is and voices gratitude for this often.

Mothering is a roller coaster of emotions and even when it is good it involves struggle.

Kim is both grateful and she’s lost something.

She understands that mothering is full of contradictory feelings, all of which matter. It is messy and interrupted and loving. Kim gets maternal ambivalence.

item.title: 5 Stubborn Myths About Mental Health and Exercise
item.description:
Depression

5 Stubborn Myths About Mental Health and Exercise

Why “Just Do It” doesn’t work and what you can do instead.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Exercise is great for mental health, but it’s often much easier said than done.
  • Small movements and micro-activations still offer powerful mental health benefits.
  • You don't need an endorphin rush or extreme effort to support mental health with movement.

The prescription is everywhere: Just go for a run, hit the gym; sweat more to stress less. While the connection between movement and mental health is well established, anyone navigating anxiety or trying to exercise with depression may find traditional fitness advice exhausting rather than healing. “Lifestyle” medicine can sound like a luxury beyond reach. The wellness social media sphere is packed with rigid rules and half-truths that can make working out feel like just another chore—or worse, make you feel like a failure if you can't keep up.

If you’ve ever struggled to get moving while dealing with anxiety or depression, and you’re tired of hearing the same unhelpful advice, it’s time to bust a few common exercise myths and find a more compassionate approach to movement.

Source: Shot Prime Studio/Shutterstock

Myth 1: Working out gives you an instant energy boost.

The Reality: Exercise actually makes you physically and mentally tired, especially high-intensity workouts or when you're just starting back up.

While it's true that long-term cardiovascular and strength gains lead to better overall energy—and a post-workout glow can feel invigorating—movement isn't a magical, instantly reversed equation. Sometimes, a workout just feels like a slog. Expecting boundless energy right away is a fast track to burnout.

Myth 2: You need frequent, intense workouts to see mental health benefits.

The Reality: The classic prescription of 30 to 45 minutes, three to five times a week, is great if you can manage it. But it is far from the only way movement supports your mind.

Any movement counts. Standing up from your desk, taking a short walk, or doing a few minutes of stretching activates your neuromuscular junctions and offers a mental reset. If you are battling depression or anxiety, the smallest shifts—moving your fingers and toes, sitting up, or raising your heels—are powerful first steps in a clinical approach called behavioral activation. You don't need a grueling training session to benefit.

Myth 3: You need to get a “runner’s high” for exercise to improve mental health.

The Reality: That euphoric endorphin rush isn't universal. It tends to show up more with longer workouts and heavily conditioned bodies. For many, exercise doesn't feel euphoric at all—it can be uncomfortable or painful.

Research shows that while intense workouts can be effective for mood, lighter activities like walking, yoga, or strength training offer powerful benefits without requiring extreme effort—and they are often much easier to maintain over time. Endorphins are real, but exercise also helps your mental health through brain growth factors, reduced inflammation, better sleep, and simply giving your mind a break from negative thought loops. It also provides a feeling of agency—of doing something. If a workout hurts or feels awful, finding something that feels the least awful is a valid starting point.

Any movement can help mental health.
Source: Kimberrywood/Shutterstock

Myth 4: Exercise can prevent or manage most anxiety and depression on its own.

The Reality: While studies show that regular exercise can rival some medications for mild-to-moderate depression, real life is messy. Maintaining study-level workout routines is hard, access to safe exercise varies wildly, and for severe depression, movement is simply not a substitute for medication or therapy.

Furthermore, high-intensity workouts that spike your heart rate can actually increase anxiety for some people. Telling someone struggling with mental health that "movement is all you need" is invalidating. Many people who exercise regularly still benefit immensely from a comprehensive treatment plan that includes professional support.

Myth 5: If you stop moving, you lose all your progress.

The Reality: Your body doesn't forget the history of movement. While your muscles and cardiovascular system can become deconditioned or stiff after a break, the physiological and psychological memory of movement remains. Dropping the "all-or-nothing" mindset makes it much easier to return to physical activity after a hiatus without shame.

Takeaway Tips

  • Move something, somewhere, somehow. Any movement is better than none.
  • Rest when you need to, especially when starting or returning to a routine.
  • Find something you actually enjoy (or at least don't dread).
  • You don't have to wait. It is OK to seek professional mental health support while trying to move more. You never have to "prove" you've tried hard enough on your own before asking for help.

item.title: 2 Signs Your Child Is Minutes Away From a Meltdown
item.description:
Cognition

2 Signs Your Child Is Minutes Away From a Meltdown

Spot these signals in your child to help you respond before emotional overload.

Posted October 26, 2026

Key points
  • Most children show warning signs before they blow up with anger.
  • Instead of arguing whether a problem is “really a big deal,” try recognizing what is happening underneath it.
  • Narrower wording is another red flag that a meltdown may be coming; being warm and flexible could stop it.

Just the other day, during a counseling session, Beth, who is the mother of 10-year-old Daniel, before she even sat down, said, “It came out of nowhere.” Obviously curious, I asked Beth (I am using different names for both her and Daniel) what she meant. Beth described to me how the day before, one minute Daniel “seemed fine” and then the next minute there was a "whole lot of screaming" from Daniel in response to Beth attempting to limit his screen time. As if the yelling was not stressful enough, for an encore, Daniel reportedly kept his meltdown going with crying, door slamming, and big-time arguing, followed by the silence of a complete emotional shutdown.

After more than 35 years of working with children and families, I have found that child meltdowns such as Daniel's rarely come out of nowhere. Most children show warning signs before they become emotionally reactive. This post is about how to spot and manage those warning signs, or what are often referred to as "red flags," before they get out of hand.

Below are two important red flags that your child may be approaching the point of emotional overload. Let me stress that while the emphasis of this post is about younger children from the ages of 6 through preteens, it can also apply to teens, and even adult children who tend to be less able to have calm, constructive conversations (what I often call being on the "bottle it up and explode later plan").

Red Flag #1: Small Problems Suddenly Feel Huge

For a younger child, a small problem that becomes disproportionately huge could be a sibling sitting in their spot. Or, for pretty much any age, as in the case of Daniel, asking a child to stop playing a video game could cause more than mild annoyance.

Yet in many cases, the precipitating situation can be even more layered. Recently, a parent shared with me about their 12-year-old daughter who lost it over not being able to find the right sweatshirt that she wanted to wear to an extended family picnic. As backstory, this same girl had confided in me some significant body image concerns and how she treasured that sweatshirt that she felt more comfortable wearing. She especially wanted to wear it to the upcoming family gathering because a not-very-tactful aunt who would also be attending recently told this girl that she had gained some weight.

The common catalyst for reactivity in all the above examples is that when the child is emotionally overloaded, any small disappointment can suddenly feel enormous. And, that is where I hear parents and children themselves recount those meltdown-specific phrases such as:

“This is totally unfair and it's my worst day ever!”

“Why does everyone hate me?”

“You never let me do anything!”

Where parents fall down is focusing on the content of what the upset child is saying rather than what the child is actually thinking and feeling. Usually, lurking under the surface are overthinking loops that are gathering speed and intensity. As I wrote in my book, 24 Hours to a Less Reactive Child, the intensity of the reaction often tells you more than the actual problem.

If you picture your child's nervous system as a cup that has been slowly filling throughout the day, you will be more able to see what is really going on under the surface. Stressors such as school pressure, friendship problems, being tired, hunger, embarrassment, sensory overload, worries, or you name it, may already have filled the cup almost to the top. And then "wham!", the missing sweatshirt is simply the final drop.

So, to all you rational parents out there, instead of arguing about whether the problem is “really a big deal,” try recognizing what is happening underneath it. For example, you might calmly say, “This situation seems like it is hitting you really hard right now.” Hopefully, you can see that such a response is not about agreement with your child's unreasonable behavior. Rather, it means you are noticing the emotional storm (and calming your child by helping them feel understood) before trying to minimize or even solve the problem.

Red Flag #2: Your Child's Language Becomes More Narrow

You are likely well-aware that when your child is becoming overwhelmed, their thinking often becomes narrower and more rigid. That takes us to a second warning sign that I often hear about when children and parents unpack meltdown episodes is a sudden loss of seeing (and wording) things as more flexible. The signs of this more rigid, narrower view are your child demanding that things happen "now," or in a certain way, or that they are like a broken record pushing you for a "yes'" to their requests. If you are like most parents, you then give even more explanations (in an attempt to broaden the child's reasoning), which often make things worse.

Some familiar sound bites of what these parents say are:

“But I already explained why, how many ways do I need to tell you the answer is no?”

“We talked about it, it is not happening and, you already knew we can't do that tonight.”

“Why are you making such a big deal about this?”

These parent explanations are reasonable, but when your child's emotional temperature rises, your greatest influence often comes from resisting the urge to rise with them. To get concrete and practical, in contrast to the typical parent responses above, try lowering your voice, using fewer words (think "less is more"), and staying warm but firm. For example, you could say, “I can see you're really upset. The answer is still not today, and I'm here when you're ready.”

The Takeaway

When you learn to spot meltdown warning signs earlier, you may have a much better chance of helping your child calm back down before the emotional storm takes over. To be clear, you are not going to prevent every meltdown. But being on the lookout for small problems that feel huge and your child's narrower thinking can be strong signals for you to respond with empathy and reasonable boundaries. By doing so, you can help your child gradually learn that intense feelings can exist without needing to control everyone around them.
